newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: FEATURE - Save the wildlife -- eat them.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Save the wildlife -- eat them.

text.p: Australian wildlife expert Grahame Webb sees a simple, but controversial, solution to saving the world's endangered animals: eat them, skin them or sell them.
Webb, an internationally-respected biologist and consultant to governments and major companies, believes the continued existence of threatened animals lies in making them worth money.
Australian favourites such as the kangaroo, koala, platypus and rare birds could all be harvested, regardless of the sensitivities of some conservationists and sections of the community, Webb says.
And vital to this is keeping the bushlands, swamps and jungles animals need to live and breed.

"At the very least, you can give landowners some incentive, some commercial incentive to pursue conservation more than they are able to do today," Webb told Reuters at his crocodile farm in this tropical capital of Australia's outback Northern Territory.
"Those people are totally committed to a certain chunk of land and they've got to earn a certain amount of money off that land," he said.

"If they can't do it because people in the cities aren't prepared to pay more for sheep and more for bread and more for milk and all the other things, then what happens is that the incentives to rape and pillage get bigger and bigger, so people put more stock on their land, people put more area under crop."
Webb sees all animals as suitable for what he calls his sustainable conservation strategy.
But first he must overcome a deep resistance among many Australians against eating beloved national symbols.
Webb, through his Wildlife Management International Pty Ltd consultancy, has prepared reports for the national and territory governments recommending sustainable harvesting.
Many of his ideas have been adopted by the Territory government in a draft strategy for sustainable use of wildlife.
"We view it (sustainable use of wildlife) as one way of achieving conservation goals," the territory's deputy director of parks and wildlife, Bill Freeland, told Reuters.
Webb's research was backed this month by a new report prepared for the national government by ACIL Economics Pty Ltd, suggesting a farming and export programme for native animals.
"Permitting the commercial use of native birds and reptiles within strict rules can contribute to the national economy," the company's report said.

"Surplus young offspring of common species such as galahs (Australian cockatoos) and long-necked tortoises, which are readily available on the domestic market and yet valuable overseas, could be harvested and reared on farms.
"This would be a precursor to initiating the main conservation benefit of ranching more valuable species, such as Major Mitchel cockatoos in conjunction with preservation of habitat."
Webb also has his critics, with passion equal to his own.
The director of the Australian office of the Humane Society International, Michael Kennedy, said there was no evidence that making animals worth money had any conservation use.
"Historically, around the world, utilisation has resulted in a decline of thousands and thousands of species," Kennedy said.
"The assumption that a farmer will protect a habitat just because there are a few parrots is really far-fetched."

Opening a legal trade in rare animals created an uncontrollable surge in demand and allowed smugglers to disguise their operations, said Kennedy, a member of Environment Minister Robert Hill's advisory council on biological diversity.
"Export trade is dangerous, it's hard to control, expensive and cruel," Kennedy said.

Webb and the Northern Territory government also see sustainable conservation as integral to protecting and maintaining the 40,000-year-old culture of Australia's native aborigines, who own large tracts of the rugged territory.
Sustainable conservation would also help aboriginal communities survive economically in the desolate outback.
